posts.author: JohnFP
posts.content_md:
Ok, I am going to have to interject.

I believe we could all learn from what he did with the "touched up" photographs. There is no physical way possible in the world to portray a hologram with a single still picture. What he did, give the viewers (holographers and non holographers) a sense of 3Dism.

The touched up Vase almost looks like a hologram for those of us lucky enough to have seen a hologram in person. For a person whom has never seen a hologram, a flat ordinary photo of a vase really doesn't do the art justice.

As holographers, we know that the image cannot go past the film. But how else do your represent 3D without a foreground reference?

So with that I have to stick up for Terry and think it's yet another excellent technique in trying to show what a hologram is with a flat picture.

BWDIK?

posts.author: MichaelH
posts.content_md:
It's a valid argument which leads me to the question...

Do the uninitiated care?

I care. But then, I know that a hologram doesn't "stick out" from the glass the way he implies it does. Seen from the side, you won't see a monster coming out of the XYZ hologram. You won't see the edges of the lady's hat covering the frame.

Do people who don't live and breath holography care? Probably not. I do though and don't think it does the field any good to portray holograms doing things that holograms don't do. It just risks people being disappointed when they do finally see something like the monster and realizing that it doesn't look in real life like it looked in the photo.

posts.author: JohnFP
posts.content_md:
Well then I guess the questions are; Should the picture not be touched up to represent a 3D image and thus the unsavvy will never be interested, never care about and never know what a hologram really is. Or should the picture be touched up, it excites the non holographer, he want to find out more about them and researches the medium. To his delight they are truely 3D and some that are image planed do stick out in front of the film.

I wonder how long it will take him/her to realize when looking at the hologram from the side, that part not in front of the film disappears. I don't think this will disapoint that person too much.

Now on the other hand, if one was selling a hologram instead of just photographiing it as Terry is doing, I would say it is the reponsibilty of the seller to explain what is happening. If the picture is touched up as Terry's is and the hologram is trying to be sold. Then an explaination as to what photography does to a hologram, why the photo was touched up and what they potential buyer can expect should be made very clear. Ie. - This photo was altered to simmulate the 3D properties a hologram has as the 3D properties are lost when a regular 2D photograph is take of it. This hologram image does stick out in front of the plate by 2 inches but only when the film plate is directly behind the image. Or something like that.

I guess why I am defending his work is when I look at the vase, it actually makes me think I am almost looking at a real hologram. Then when I look at the beautiful work done by Fred U or Jon M as photos, they look just like beautiful flat spirographs of colors with no depth and no indication of what they truely are. It is only my experience with holograms that allows me to mentally envision what they may look like in real life.

posts.author: BobH
posts.content_md:
> Do people who don't live and breath holography care? Probably not.

*I care.* I think it's a real shame that this typical photographic fraud was allowed to be displayed by holography community. It suggests to the casual observer that we support it. 

I consider it an insult. It's a slap in the face for anyone who has ever tried to explain the difference between real holography and Princess Leia hollywood effects. It's a total misrepresentation of the artwork (and medium) he photographed. If I were the artist of the work he modified to (in *his* mind) improve, I'd demand it not be published.

Shame on those who saw it and used it!

posts.author: JohnFP
posts.content_md:
> I care. I think it's a real shame that this typical photographic fraud was allowed to be displayed by holography community. It suggests to the casual observer that we support it.I consider it an insult. It's a slap in the face for anyone who has ever tried to explain the difference between real holography and Princess Leia hollywood effects. It's a total misrepresentation of the artwork (and medium) he photographed. If I were the artist of the work he modified to (in his mind) improve, I'd demand it not be published.

Bob, I wish I saw it your way, but I don't. I don't think his modifications are any more of a misrepresentation of the artwork then a plain photograph is. A plain photograph kills the essence of what a hologram is in real life. Comparing apples to oranges, the princess lea hologram was in a 3D medium in my eyes, X-Y-Time. To take a photograph of a hologram and compare it to the aminational recording of a movie is just as bad as altering the photo. 

Does this do the Leia hologam justice? How many observers would see this photo and say, "WOW, holograms are cool?"

![Image](http://www.adukes.demon.co.uk/cards/swt-l1.jpg)

Or this one.

![Image](http://www.brainwise.org/Images/LeiaHologramGrab5.jpg)

If we are to demand those type of photos not be published we should demand all single photo shots of holograms not be published because they are gross misrepresentations of what a real hologram is also. We should, as holographer only use and only allow a movie of a hologram or a 3D representation (stereo images etc..) of the hologram. 

I am sorry I do not agree with you but until a better form of photography can justify the essence of a hologram I see the altered photos not worst then the unaltered ones. 

We are not going to change the publics viewpoint of the hologram, but we can represent our work in such a way that is captures their interest. Expecially since most holograms are monochromatic which makes picture taking of them even worst.

Just my humble opinion and it does not mean to disrepect yours.

posts.author: BobH
posts.content_md:
> I don't think his modifications are any more of a misrepresentation of the artwork then a plain photograph is.

What about framing, or the size of the head relative to the frame? He obviously made a good photo of the artwork as it was intentionally framed (cropped), so why did he need to modify the image? A plain photograph (even if in black & white) would have been an accurate representation of the image as seen by a one-eyed person. 

> the princess lea hologram

What princess leia hologram? Is there a definition of "hologram" that describes the special effect pictured? 

> the princess lea hologram was in a 3D medium in my eyes, X-Y-Time. To take a photograph of a hologram and compare it to the aminational recording of a movie is just as bad as altering the photo.

If you mean to say that a single frame from a movie is to the movie, as an altered photograph of a hologram is to the hologram, I disagree. The former is a sample of the real thing, the latter has creative input from the photographer. 

Also, the photo we're talking about wasn't in some marketing pitch (which is bad enough), it was in the context of what was on display at the holography conference (giving validity to the lie). 

Again, why was it necessary? Perhaps the photographer had dimensional envy? 

> If we are to demand those type of photos not be published we should demand all single photo shots of holograms not be published because they are gross misrepresentations of what a real hologram is also.

Again, I think they're single perspective views of the real thing. 

> We are not going to change the publics viewpoint of the hologram, but we can represent our work in such a way that is captures their interest.

I certainly agree with *that*! I just don't think marketing BS is appropriate in the context we're discussing. Just *my* opinion as well, but I'm someone "who lives and breathes holography".
